why_how.text: When you pull out from a parked or stopped position, the manual puts the duty to yield on you.
Parallel parking has a set direction and a set curb distance that you need to know exactly.

scenario.text: You are parked at a curb with your signal on, and a car is approaching in the lane you want to enter.

reasoning.text: Signaling does not make other traffic yield to you; you yield to all other traffic.

result.text: You let the car pass, check your mirrors and blind spots again, then pull out.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a turn signal gives you the right to pull out of a parking spot.

correction.text: Traffic does not have to yield to you because you signaled; you yield to all other traffic.

memory_support.text: Face the flow, twelve inches from the curb.

prompt.text: When you parallel park next to a curb, what is the most your wheels may be from it?

rationale.text: You park parallel to the curb and no more than twelve inches from it.

lines.text: Know the direction and the distance.

narration.text: This lesson covers the everyday parking skills: pulling out of a space, parallel parking and angle parking. The first rule applies every single time you leave a parked or stopped position, and it is about other traffic, not about you. Then we look at how to line your vehicle up when you parallel park, including the exact distance from the curb, and what changes when there is no curb at all. Finally we cover marked spaces and angle parking, including a special caution for drivers of large vehicles. Each of these has a rule you can learn exactly.

When you pull out from a parked or stopped position, check your mirrors and your blind spots, and yield to all other traffic. That last part is absolute. Every other vehicle on the road goes before you. Before pulling out from a parked or stopped spot, check mirrors and blind spots and yield to all other traffic. So check, find your gap, and then pull out into traffic. Mirrors and blind spots first, then a gap, then you pull out.

lines.text: No more than twelve inches from the curb.
No curb: close to the shoulder edge.

narration.text: When parallel parking, face the same direction that traffic moves in that lane. Then park parallel to the curb and no more than twelve inches from it. If there is no curb, park as close as you can to the edge of the shoulder. Notice the difference between those two cases. With a curb you stay within twelve inches of it, but with no curb you simply get as close as you can to the shoulder edge, with no set number. Where parking spaces are marked, your wheels must be inside the marked space. Those are the full lining-up rules.

lines.text: Check mirrors and blind spots first.
You still yield to all traffic.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver at the curb starts to pull out from a parked or stopped position without checking blind spots first, expecting approaching cars to slow down and let them in. That is not how it works. Before pulling out from a parked or stopped spot, check mirrors and blind spots and yield to all other traffic. The decision to go depends on checking your mirrors and blind spots and finding a safe gap so no other traffic has to give way to you.

lines.text: Angle parking in lots and wide streets.
Large vehicles: do not block traffic.

narration.text: The manual's parallel parking steps are to pull even with the car labeled Car A, back slowly into the space while turning the wheels sharply, and then straighten the wheels. Angle parking is the other common type. It is common in parking lots, at shopping centers and on wide streets. When driving a large vehicle, avoid angle spaces where your vehicle would stick out and block traffic on the road. Signs may also show that an angle parking area is reverse angle or back-in only, so read the signs before you pull in. Read them first.

Here is a quick check: you are parallel parking on a street with a curb. What is the most your wheels may be from the curb? The answer is twelve inches. You park parallel to the curb and no more than twelve inches from it. Keep the no-curb case separate: if there is no curb, you park as close as you can to the edge of the shoulder, and there is no set number for that. Either way, face the same direction that traffic moves in that lane, and keep your wheels inside any marked space. Those two facts together cover every curb situation.

lines.text: Face traffic flow, within twelve inches.

narration.text: To pull the basics together: when you leave a parked or stopped position, check mirrors and blind spots and yield to all other traffic. When you parallel park, face the same direction as traffic in that lane, stay within twelve inches of the curb, or as close as you can to the shoulder edge with no curb, and keep your wheels inside marked spaces. Angle parking is common in lots, shopping centers and wide streets, large vehicles should avoid spaces where they would block the road, and signs may mark back-in only areas.

why_how.text: On a hill, a parked vehicle that rolls can end up in traffic, so the brake, the gear and the wheels all matter.
The wheel direction depends on whether you face uphill or downhill and whether there is a curb, which makes it easy to mix up.

scenario.text: You park facing uphill on a street with a curb.

reasoning.text: Parked uphill next to a curb, the front wheels turn toward the travel lane.

result.text: You set the parking brake, leave the car in gear or park, and turn the wheels toward the travel lane.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the wheels always turn toward the curb when you park on a hill.

correction.text: Only downhill at a curb do the wheels point toward the curb; uphill at a curb they point toward the travel lane.

memory_support.text: Down to the curb, up to the lane, no curb to the edge.

prompt.text: You park facing downhill with a curb beside you. Which way do the front wheels point?

rationale.text: Parked downhill next to a curb, you turn your front wheels toward the curb.

lines.text: Keep the car out of traffic.

narration.text: Parking on a hill adds a risk that flat ground does not have: if something fails, the vehicle can roll. The manual's hill parking rules are built to stop that from ending up in traffic. There are three parts. First, how you set the parking brake and the transmission. Second, why you turn the front wheels at all. Third, which way to turn them, which depends on whether you face uphill or downhill and whether there is a curb. Learners usually remember that the wheels turn, but forget which way, so we will drill that carefully.

lines.text: Manual in gear, automatic in park.

narration.text: When parking on a hill, always set the parking brake. Then use the transmission as a second layer of protection: leave a manual transmission in gear, or an automatic transmission in park. So on a hill the parking brake is always set, and the gear selection differs only by transmission, in gear for a manual and in park for an automatic. On top of the brake and the gear, you turn your front wheels so the vehicle would not roll downhill into traffic if the brake failed. That is the reason behind every wheel direction in this lesson.

lines.text: Downhill at a curb: toward the curb.
Uphill at a curb: toward the lane.
No curb: toward the road edge.

narration.text: There are three cases. Parked downhill next to a curb, turn your front wheels toward the curb. Parked uphill next to a curb, turn your front wheels toward the travel lane. Parked on a hill with no curb, turn your front wheels toward the edge of the road. Without a curb, the front wheels point toward the road edge whether the vehicle faces uphill or downhill. So the slope only changes the answer when there is a curb; with no curb, it is always the road edge. Saying the three cases together helps you keep them straight.

lines.text: Uphill at a curb is different.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers learn one hill rule, turn the wheels toward the curb, and use it everywhere. That is only right when you face downhill next to a curb. Facing downhill at a curb the front wheels point toward the curb, while facing uphill at a curb they point toward the travel lane. If you get the uphill case wrong, the wheels are no longer doing their job of keeping the vehicle from rolling downhill into traffic if the brake fails. So before you turn the wheel, ask two questions: am I facing uphill or downhill, and is there a curb?

Here is a quick check: you park facing downhill, and there is a curb right beside your car. Which way do you turn the front wheels? The answer is toward the curb. Parked downhill next to a curb, the front wheels turn toward the curb. Compare the other two cases so you do not mix them up: facing uphill at a curb, the wheels turn toward the travel lane, and with no curb at all, the wheels turn toward the edge of the road whether you face uphill or downhill. And in every case, the parking brake is set. Brake, gear and wheels, every time.

lines.text: Down to curb, up to lane, no curb to edge.

narration.text: To finish, put the whole routine together every time you park on a slope. Set the parking brake. Leave a manual transmission in gear or an automatic in park. Then turn the front wheels so the vehicle would not roll downhill into traffic if the brake failed: toward the curb when you face downhill at a curb, toward the travel lane when you face uphill at a curb, and toward the edge of the road when there is no curb, whichever way you face. Brake, gear and wheels together give you three separate protections on a hill.

why_how.text: Disabled parking spaces are reserved by law, and parking in one without a permit is expensive even for a short stop.
The no-stopping places have one narrow exception, and knowing its limits keeps you from relying on it wrongly.

scenario.text: You want to pull into a disabled space for a few minutes to grab something from a store, and you have no permit.

reasoning.text: Parking there without a valid permit is illegal, with fines from one hundred sixty-five dollars up to one thousand dollars, even for a few minutes.

result.text: You park in a regular space instead.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a quick stop in a disabled space is not a violation.

correction.text: The fines apply even if you park there only a few minutes.

memory_support.text: No permit, no parking, not even a minute.

prompt.text: What is the lowest fine for parking in a disabled space without a permit?

rationale.text: Fines for parking in a disabled space without a permit start at one hundred sixty-five dollars and can reach one thousand dollars.

lines.text: Rules apply in or out of the car.

narration.text: This lesson covers two things that often surprise drivers. The first is how strictly disabled parking spaces are protected, including what the fines are. The second is a pair of general facts about the whole list of places where you may not stop or park: those rules apply whether or not you are sitting in the vehicle, and there is only one narrow exception to them, a breakdown. Knowing both keeps you from assuming that a short stop, or staying behind the wheel, makes a banned spot acceptable, because neither one does.

lines.text: Permits for people and transport groups.
Symbol on the ground and a sign.

narration.text: Oregon issues special parking permits to people with disabilities and to groups that transport people with disabilities. The spaces themselves are easy to recognize. A disabled parking space may show the disability symbol painted on the ground as well as a sign with the symbol at the front of the space. Parking in a space marked for people with disabilities is illegal unless you have a valid disabled parking permit. So the test is simple: a valid permit, or no parking in that space, whatever the situation or the time of day.

lines.text: Fines start at one hundred sixty-five dollars.
They can reach one thousand dollars.

narration.text: The manual is direct about the cost. Parking in a disabled space without a Disabled Person Parking Permit brings fines that start at one hundred sixty-five dollars and can reach one thousand dollars, even if you park there only a few minutes. That last part closes the most common excuse. There is no grace period for a quick errand. The fines apply to the act of parking there without a permit, not to how long you stay. So a short stop costs the same kind of fine as a long one, and the space stays reserved for permit holders.

lines.text: Errands do not excuse the rules.
Only a breakdown that leaves you stuck.

narration.text: Here is the trap, and it covers more than disabled spaces. A driver thinks that staying in the car, or stopping only for a moment, makes a banned place acceptable. It does not. Parking and stopping rules apply whether or not you are inside the vehicle. The no-stopping and no-parking places do not apply only when your vehicle breaks down and cannot be moved out of the traffic lanes, or when the shoulder has no room for you to pull off. The list is waived only for a breakdown like that, not for a short errand. A stuck vehicle is the only exception.

Here is a quick check: a driver without a permit parks in a disabled space for a few minutes. What is the lowest fine the manual lists for that? The answer is one hundred sixty-five dollars. Parking in a disabled space without a Disabled Person Parking Permit brings fines that start at one hundred sixty-five dollars and can reach one thousand dollars, even if the driver stayed only a few minutes. A short stay does not change the rule, and only a valid disabled parking permit makes parking in that space legal. Permit or no parking.

lines.text: Rules apply in or out of the car.

narration.text: To wrap up, remember three points. Disabled spaces, marked with the symbol on the ground and a sign at the front, are for drivers with a valid disabled parking permit, and Oregon issues those permits to people with disabilities and groups that transport them. Without a permit, fines run from one hundred sixty-five dollars to one thousand dollars, even for a few minutes. And for every no-stopping place, the rules apply whether or not you are in the car, with the only exception being a breakdown that leaves you stuck in the lanes or with no room on the shoulder.

why_how.text: The manual lists by name the places where you may not stop or park, from traffic lanes to sidewalks to fire hydrants.
The list bans stopping, not just parking, which changes what counts as a violation.

scenario.text: You want to drop a friend off by stopping next to a car already parked at the curb.

reasoning.text: Stopping on the road side of a vehicle that is already parked is double parking, and it is not allowed.

result.text: You find a legal space at the curb instead of stopping beside the parked car.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the no-parking list only stops you from parking, not from a brief stop.

correction.text: Every place on the no-parking list, the ten-foot fire hydrant zone included, bans stopping as well as parking.

memory_support.text: Lanes, corners, walkways, tracks, bridges, driveways, hydrants.

prompt.text: A fire hydrant sits at the curb where you want to park. What is the closest you may park to it?

rationale.text: You may not park within ten feet of a fire hydrant, and that zone bans stopping as well as parking.

lines.text: Some places are always off limits.

narration.text: The manual gives a list of places where you may not stop or park, and it is worth knowing item by item, because each place is named on the list and none has a time allowance. Some are in the road itself, some are where people walk or ride, some are structures like bridges and tunnels, and some are about access, such as driveways and fire hydrants. One fact covers the whole list: every place on it bans stopping as well as parking. So the question is never whether you will be there long, but whether the place is on the list.

Start with the road itself. You may not stop or park in a traffic lane of a highway, street or road, or inside an intersection. Double parking is also banned. Double parking means stopping on the road side of a vehicle that is already parked, and it is not allowed. All three are on the list by name. So a traffic lane of a highway, street or road, the inside of an intersection, and the road side of a parked vehicle are never places to stop or park, whether you are in the vehicle or not. Double parking means stopping on the road side of a parked vehicle.

lines.text: No sidewalks, crosswalks or bike lanes.

narration.text: Next come the places people walk and ride, and places that are dangerous or hard to clear. You may not stop or park on a sidewalk, crosswalk, bicycle lane or path, or on any railroad or light rail tracks. You may not stop or park on a bridge or overpass, in a tunnel, or between the separate roadways of a divided highway. And you may not stop or park near construction or road work where your vehicle would interfere with traffic. Each of these is on the list by name, so there is no gray area for any of them. Learn each place by name.

lines.text: Not where signs or markings forbid.
Ten feet from a fire hydrant.

narration.text: The last items are about access. You may not stop or park in front of a public or private driveway, or anywhere that signs, traffic control devices, diagonal stripes or other road markings forbid it. And you may not park within ten feet of a fire hydrant. The hydrant zone is a fixed distance of ten feet. Driveways, public or private, are on the list by name. Signs, traffic control devices, diagonal stripes and other road markings mark the other places where stopping or parking is forbidden. And remember that every place on the list bans stopping too.

Here is the trap. A driver pulls up next to a fire hydrant to wait for a passenger, engine running, thinking that a stop is not the same as parking. On this list, it is. Every place on the no-parking list, the ten-foot fire hydrant zone included, bans stopping as well as parking. The same goes for a traffic lane, an intersection, a crosswalk or the road side of a parked car. Waiting with the engine running in one of these places is still a violation, because the list covers stopping, not only leaving the vehicle. Find a legal spot instead.

lines.text: A fire hydrant at the curb.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: there is a fire hydrant at the curb where you want to park. How close to it may you park? The answer is no closer than ten feet. You may not park within ten feet of a fire hydrant. Remember that this zone is on the no-parking list, so it bans stopping as well as parking; pulling up there to wait for someone is not allowed either. The same is true of every place on the list, from traffic lanes and intersections to sidewalks, bike lanes, tracks, bridges, tunnels and driveways. Learn the whole list by name.

lines.text: No stopping, not just no parking.

narration.text: To review the full list: no stopping or parking in a traffic lane, inside an intersection, or on the road side of a parked vehicle. None on a sidewalk, crosswalk, bicycle lane or path, or on railroad or light rail tracks. None on a bridge or overpass, in a tunnel, or between the separate roadways of a divided highway, and none near road work where you would interfere with traffic. None in front of a driveway or where signs or markings forbid it, and no parking within ten feet of a hydrant. Every item bans stopping as well as parking.

why_how.text: Several no-parking rules use fixed distances from fire stations, crosswalks, signals and railroad tracks.
Some distances share a number but carry different conditions, which is where test mistakes happen.

scenario.text: You want to park across the street from a fire station driveway.

reasoning.text: Near a fire station driveway the limit is fifteen feet on the same side of the street but seventy-five feet on the opposite side.

result.text: Because you are on the opposite side, you park at least seventy-five feet away from the driveway.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking both fifty-foot rules only apply when a sign would be hidden.

correction.text: The fifty-foot rule near a signal or sign applies only when you would hide it, but the fifty-foot railroad crossing rule always applies.

memory_support.text: Fifteen same side, seventy-five across, twenty from a crosswalk.

prompt.text: There is an unmarked crosswalk at the corner where you want to park. What is the closest you may park to it?

answer.text: No closer than twenty feet, marked or unmarked.

rationale.text: You may not park within twenty feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, whether the crosswalk is marked or unmarked.

narration.text: Many parking rules come with a measured distance, and each distance is tied to a specific object: a fire station driveway, a crosswalk, a traffic signal or sign, a railroad crossing, or the tracks themselves. Some of these distances always apply. Others apply only under a condition, such as hiding a sign or interfering with a train. In this lesson we go through each one with its number and its condition, and then we compare the rules that share a number, because those are the ones that are easiest to confuse when you are answering questions.

lines.text: Fire station: fifteen feet same side.
Seventy-five feet on the opposite side.

narration.text: You may not park within fifteen feet of a fire station driveway on the same side of the street, or within seventy-five feet of it on the opposite side. So near a fire station driveway the limit is fifteen feet on the same side but seventy-five feet on the opposite side; the larger number is across the street. You may not park within twenty feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, whether the crosswalk is marked or unmarked. An unmarked crosswalk counts just the same, so the twenty-foot rule applies at intersections with no painted lines.

lines.text: Signal or sign: fifty feet if hidden.
Railroad crossing: fifty feet from the rail.
Tracks: seven and a half feet if interfering.

narration.text: You may not park within fifty feet of a traffic signal or sign if your vehicle would hide it from view. At a railroad or light rail crossing, keep your parked vehicle at least fifty feet from the closest rail. Along the tracks there is a separate rule: you may not park within seven and a half feet of railroad or light rail tracks when your vehicle would interfere with a train. So the fifty-foot crossing rule is measured from the nearest rail, while the seven and a half foot rule applies along any tracks only when you would interfere with a train.

lines.text: Signal or sign: only if hidden.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two rules use fifty feet, and drivers merge them into one. The fifty-foot rule near a traffic signal or sign applies only when your vehicle would hide it from view, unlike the railroad crossing rule of the same distance, which always applies. So for a signal or sign, the question is whether your vehicle would hide it; for a railroad crossing, you keep at least fifty feet from the closest rail every time. Same number, different condition: hiding the signal or sign matters for one, and not for the other.

The fire station rule has its own version of this trap. Drivers remember fifteen feet and apply it everywhere around the station. That is right only on the same side of the street as the driveway. On the opposite side, the limit grows to seventy-five feet. Near a fire station driveway the limit is fifteen feet on the same side of the street but seventy-five feet on the opposite side. So before you park near a fire station, check which side of the street you are on, then apply the matching distance from its driveway.

Here is a quick check: you want to park near a crosswalk at an intersection, and the crosswalk has no painted lines. How close to it may you park? The answer is no closer than twenty feet. You may not park within twenty feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, whether the crosswalk is marked or unmarked. The missing paint does not change the distance. Keep it separate from the hydrant distance of ten feet and the fire station distances of fifteen feet on the same side and seventy-five feet on the opposite side. Tie each distance to its object.

lines.text: Fifty if hidden, fifty from the rail.
Seven and a half if interfering.

narration.text: Here are the distances from this lesson together. Fifteen feet from a fire station driveway on the same side, seventy-five feet on the opposite side. Twenty feet from a crosswalk at an intersection, marked or unmarked. Fifty feet from a traffic signal or sign, but only if your vehicle would hide it. Fifty feet from the closest rail at a railroad or light rail crossing, always. And seven and a half feet from railroad or light rail tracks when your vehicle would interfere with a train. Tie each number to its object and its condition.

why_how.text: A breakdown can force you to stop where stopping is normally banned, and the manual sets conditions for that.
A stopped vehicle that is hard to see needs warnings far enough out for other drivers to react.
Leaving a vehicle unattended has its own four steps.

scenario.text: Your car breaks down around a curve where approaching drivers cannot see it from two hundred feet away.

reasoning.text: When your stopped vehicle cannot be seen from two hundred feet in each direction, you warn drivers with flags, flares, signs, signals or flaggers at least two hundred feet out both ways.

result.text: You turn on your hazard lights and set out warning devices at least two hundred feet from the car in both directions.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking hazard lights alone are always enough after a breakdown.

correction.text: Hazard lights are the warning for any breakdown stop, and when the vehicle cannot be seen from two hundred feet each way you add warning devices.

memory_support.text: Engine off, key out, brakes set, flashers on.

prompt.text: Before you walk away from a vehicle you must leave unattended, what four things do you do?

answer.text: Turn off the engine, take out the key, set the brakes and switch on the hazard lights.

rationale.text: The manual lists those four steps before leaving a vehicle unattended.

narration.text: Sooner or later, many drivers have a breakdown. This lesson covers what the manual allows when that happens and what it requires of you. A breakdown can let you stop in a place where stopping is normally banned, but only under conditions. A vehicle stopped on or near the road needs to be visible, and sometimes that means setting out warning devices. Leaving a vehicle unattended has its own steps. And if a vehicle is left where parking is banned or where it creates a hazard, police can have it removed, and the cost falls on the owner.

lines.text: Short stop if there is no choice.
Shoulder if traffic can get by.

narration.text: If your vehicle breaks down and there is no other choice, you may stop or park for a short time where it is normally banned, as long as it creates no hazard, and you turn on your hazard lights. When needed, you may park on a highway shoulder if passing traffic still has enough room to get by. Each condition matters: no other choice, a short time, no hazard, hazard lights on, and room for traffic to pass. A breakdown is not permission to leave a vehicle anywhere for as long as you like. If any condition is missing, the exception does not apply.

lines.text: Hidden from two hundred feet: add devices.
Devices at least two hundred feet out.

narration.text: Hazard lights are the warning for any breakdown stop. Sometimes they are not enough. If your stopped vehicle cannot be seen from two hundred feet away in each direction, warn oncoming drivers using flags, flares, signs, signals or flaggers set out at least two hundred feet from the vehicle in both directions. So the test is whether drivers can see your vehicle from two hundred feet each way. If they can, hazard lights do the job. If they cannot, you add warning devices at least two hundred feet out on both sides of the vehicle.

lines.text: Flashers alone may not be enough.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver breaks down just past a curve, turns on the hazard lights and assumes that covers it. If approaching drivers cannot see the vehicle from two hundred feet away in each direction, hazard lights alone are not enough. The manual requires flags, flares, signs, signals or flaggers set out at least two hundred feet from the vehicle in both directions. Hazard lights are always part of the warning, but when the vehicle is hidden, you add the devices. Ask yourself whether someone two hundred feet away could see you.

lines.text: Engine off, key out, brakes, hazards.
Police may remove banned or hazardous cars.

narration.text: Before leaving a vehicle unattended, turn off the engine, take out the key, set the brakes and switch on the hazard lights. If a vehicle is left in the wrong place, there are consequences. A police officer may have a vehicle removed if it is parked where parking is banned or if it creates a hazard, and the owner pays the towing and storage costs. In other words, you are the one responsible for those costs. A vehicle left where parking is banned, or one that creates a hazard, can be removed at the owner's cost. You pay for the tow.

Here is a quick check: your car has broken down, you have moved it as safely as you can, and now you must leave it unattended to get help. What four things do you do before you walk away? The answer is to turn off the engine, take out the key, set the brakes and switch on the hazard lights. If drivers cannot see the vehicle from two hundred feet in each direction, you also set out warning devices at least two hundred feet away both ways. And remember that a car left where it creates a hazard can be towed at your cost.

lines.text: Short stop, no hazard, hazards on.
You pay if it is towed.

narration.text: To finish: if your vehicle breaks down with no other choice, you may stop briefly where it is normally banned, as long as it creates no hazard and your hazard lights are on, and you may use a highway shoulder when needed if traffic can still get by. Hazard lights are the warning for any breakdown stop, and when the vehicle cannot be seen from two hundred feet each way, you add warning devices at least two hundred feet out. Before leaving it, engine off, key out, brakes set and hazards on, and remember police may tow a vehicle left where it is banned, at your cost.
